text:
A: Hello! Yeah, Tomasz, from Walsall. You are Hetal, yeah?
B: Yes, hello. Hetal. Sorry, I'm in Neasden, London.
A: London, okay. So what do you do, Hetal?
B: Erm, I'm a tailor. Alterations. But at the moment I'm, erm, looking for work. The shop I worked in closed.
A: Ah, that's bad. How long?
B: About eighteen months now. I do some alterations for neighbours, people from the temple, but it's not regular, you know?
A: Listen, I tell you something. I came here 2006, agency, warehouse in Wednesbury. Then driving, deliveries. Then I go telesales because I realise, I can talk. Everybody finds something. Where you apply?
B: Department stores, the alterations counters. Costume companies, uniform companies. Sometimes shop work, warehouse.
A: Warehouse is easy to get. Agency, they take anybody. But money is rubbish. You tried call centre? We always hire. Always. People leave every month.
B: Erm, no. I don't think I'm good on the phone. I get very nervous, even when I phone the Jobcentre. I write notes before.
A: Notes is good! That's a script, yeah? We have script also. First week everybody is nervous. Then it's nothing.
B: Maybe. Sorry, I think I'm better with the hands. With the machine.
A: Okay, okay, fair enough. You're good with machine, you do your own thing. Like a business, yeah? From home.
B: Yes, I would like that one day. Sari blouses, properly, registered, with a little website. But now I just want a regular wage, you know? Less worry.
A: Everybody wants less worry. I say to my wife, one day I start my own business, energy broker. She says, Tomasz, you say this five years. (laughs) She's right.
B: (laughs) My mum also says things like that to me.
A: Mums, yeah. My mum is in Poland. I send her money every month. Every month. My brother, nothing. Anyway. You live with family?
B: No, I live alone. Small flat. My parents are in Harrow, I go most Sundays. And the lift in my block is broken one week, so lots of stairs.
A: Sorry? The lift?
B: Sorry, the lift. Broken for a week. Second floor, so it's okay, but with shopping bags...
A: Ah, they never fix. Same everywhere. My landlord, I ring him about the boiler, three weeks. Three weeks! And I pay rent on time, every month.
B: That's bad. In winter also.
A: Where you do your shopping? Here I go Caldmore Green, Polish shop, and there's Asian shops also, very cheap vegetables.
B: Ealing Road. Big Asian grocers. This week okra was on offer, very good. I cook for the whole week, thepla, dal.
A: Thepla, what is it?
B: Erm, like a flatbread, with fenugreek, spices. Good for taking out, it keeps.
A: Like we have pierogi, my wife makes. I do barbecue only. In summer that's my job, nobody touches it.
B: Okay. Like my dad with the cricket on TV. Nobody touches the remote.
A: Ha! Exactly. Listen, car boot sales, you go? Sunday morning. Sewing machines sometimes, cheap, tenner. Last week I got drill set for a fiver. Fiver! I sell it for twenty-five.
B: Really? I didn't think about car boot. My machine is old. Sometimes I think I need a second one, industrial, but they're very expensive.
A: Never buy new. Never. You haggle. They say thirty, you say fifteen, you walk away, they call you back. Always.
B: Erm, I'm not very good at that. I just pay what they say, sorry.
A: No, no, I teach you. First rule, you don't look too happy —
